description: We help you find a job abroad.
about_heading: We help people find jobs and build their lives in Europe.
about_text: Our mission is to simplify the path to an international career. We work with trusted employers in different European countries and guide candidates through each stage: from job search to documentation and adaptation abroad. Our experts know what it’s like to start from scratch in another country. We believe working abroad is not just employment — it's an opportunity to grow, explore the world, and change your life.
country_pl_text:
The labor legislation of the Republic of Poland
Labor law in Poland is primarily governed by the 1974 Labor Code. It regulates working conditions such as working hours, holidays, rest periods, wages, overtime, leave, termination, etc. Another relevant law is the Act on Non-Working Days of January 18, 1951.
country_de_text:
Labor legislation in Germany
Labor law in Germany is regulated by the Basic Law (Constitution), the Labor Code, and numerous federal laws and regulations. It covers aspects such as employment contracts, protection against dismissal, working hours, minimum wage, occupational safety, and collective agreements. Special attention is given to workers' rights, union activities, and protection of employees' personal data.
country_ru_text:
Labor legislation in Russia
Labor law in Russia is mainly regulated by the Labor Code of 1974. The Code governs working conditions such as working hours, holidays, rest periods, wages, overtime work, vacations, and dismissal, etc. Another important regulation is the Law on Non-Working Days of January 18, 1951.

plMain: Main requirements of the labor legislation of the Czech Republic
workTimeDesc: According to Polish labor law, working time is the period during which the employee is at the disposal of the employer. It must not exceed 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week. Taking into account overtime, the average weekly norm cannot exceed 48 hours over the calculation period.
workSystemDesc: According to Polish labor law, working time is the period during which the employee is at the disposal of the employer. It must not exceed 8 hours per day and 40 hours per week. Taking into account overtime, the average weekly norm cannot exceed 48 hours over the calculation period.
workAccountingDesc: Working time accounting must record hours worked, including night shifts, overtime, and work on weekends. In a task-based accounting system, this is not required. Records are kept for 3 years (Art. 149 of the Polish Labor Code, Art. 6 of the Regulation).
ruMain: Key labor law requirements of the Russian Federation
dworkTimeDesc: In Russia, the standard workweek is 40 hours, with a maximum of 8 hours per day. Overtime is allowed with limitations. Work on weekends and holidays is prohibited except in certain cases and must be compensated. Time tracking is mandatory.
dworkSystemDesc: Russia uses different working time systems: fixed 8-hour workday, flexible schedule, shift work, part-time work, and rotational method. The choice of system is determined by the employment contract or collective agreement.
dworkAccountingDesc: In Russia, employers are required to keep records of employees' working hours, including start and end times, breaks, overtime, and weekend work. This is necessary to ensure compliance with labor laws and correct payroll calculation. Records must be kept for at least 5 years.
